subject: research/swe-nullrate
professional: a meta-research methodologist who runs content analyses of published abstracts (the Fanelli 2010/2012 kind of study), with a statistician's eye on the intervals; first checks: is the sample really random and frozen, do the counts and Wilson intervals recompute, is there a written codebook and a second coder with kappa, would an outside coder give the same labels, and is the headline compared with the existing positive-result literature

evidence.correctness: Ran `python3 experiments/run.py` and diffed it with the committed experiments/results.txt: identical. Independent recomputation in /tmp/claude-0/nr_check.py (Wilson interval solved as the roots of the quadratic (p^ - p)^2 = z^2 p(1-p)/n with z = NormalDist().inv_cdf(0.975), not the package's closed form, and its own re-draw of random.Random(20261019).sample over sorted slugs): sample membership matches labels.tsv; counts 16/14/9/41 (also by awk); 23/39 = 58.97% [43.42%, 72.92%]; 9/39 = 23.08% [12.65%, 38.34%]; 41/80 [40.49%, 61.89%]; 229/711 [28.88%, 35.73%]; 649/711 [88.98%, 93.14%]: every README and results.txt figure matches. Keyword rule confusion matrix recounted with grep -P over a join of summaries and labels: positive 3, mixed 8, negative 7, descriptive 7 flagged, so tp 15 fp 10 fn 8 tn 47, precision 0.60, recall 0.652, as reported. Disclosure count 649 recounted with grep -ciwE. The arithmetic is right. The labels are less solid: a spot relabel of 57 of the 80 (32 mixed/descriptive read blind, 25 positive/negative read with labels visible) agreed on 28 of 32 blind, but I would move about 7 of the 25: garment-stackopt, sensing-timesync and garment-twonodeheld (each says 'but chroma falls', 'fails on a nearly still platform', 'the gain may not survive actuation lag') are labelled positive despite the README's 'boundary cases went to the less flattering class'; accel-fpga, accel-ttfit and tail-elicitation test no alternative (descriptive); chip-mac-lanes confirms the earlier sweep (not negative). Under that relabel the headline becomes 25/35 = 71% [55%, 84%], inside the reported interval's upper end, so the direction of the claim survives but the point estimate is soft.
evidence.completeness: Everything the README lists runs: 7 unit tests (pass, 0.011 s), run.py reproduces results.txt byte for byte, figure.py run in a scratch copy reproduces headline_types.svg byte for byte (cmp), tests check labels.tsv is exactly the seeded sample. data/summaries.tsv has 711 rows as stated; 671 of them are still identical to today's _homepage/projects.json (794 projects now), none removed, so the snapshot is honest. The study is marked preliminary and its next steps (second labeller, kappa, full-README labelling) are listed as not done, not claimed. The live page could not be loaded (proxy 403 for marisstella.app); the project's homepage summary in _homepage/projects.json matches the README numbers.
evidence.verification: `cd research/swe-nullrate && PYTHONPATH=src python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -v`: 7 tests, OK, 0.011 s. Six mutants with platform/ci/quality_mutate.py: caught 3 (Wilson centre z^2/(2n) -> z^2/n; false-negative count definition; sample seed +1); survived 3: dropping 'ties' from the NEG keyword rule, dropping 'assumed' from the DISCLOSE rule (the 91% headline), and run.py counting only 'negative' instead of 'negative'+'mixed' (the 59% headline). Nothing tests run.py's output against results.txt, so the two headline computations are guarded only by the author re-running the script.
evidence.craft: Read src/swe_nullrate/__init__.py (78 lines), tests/test_nullrate.py, experiments/run.py, experiments/figure.py. Small, stdlib-only, readable; the sample is asserted at run time. Defects: load_projects opens the JSON without closing it (__init__.py:31); only summaries pass through plain(), so 19 titles in data/summaries.tsv keep raw '’' entities, and at least one snapshotted summary (swe-orgs) is garbled ('checklistrsquo;s') from the source; the analysis lives in a top-level script with no function to test; SHORT (__init__.py:10) is unused.
evidence.claims: Backed by files: every count, share and interval in README and the homepage summary (recomputed above); '7 tests, well under a second'; 'tests check labels.tsv is exactly this sample'; the keyword rule's numbers and the caution against the by-theme shares; the three named negative examples (osrobot-morph, chip-macp32cells, codesign-gripper) do say so in their summaries. Limitations are unusually candid (one labeller, same model family, post-hoc rubric, truncated reading, in-sample rule). Not backed: 'Boundary cases went to the less flattering class' (README.md:31) is contradicted by at least three labels (labels.tsv:7, :24, :67); 'there is no comparable benchmark' (README.md:36) ignores Fanelli 2010 (PLoS ONE 5(4): e10068) and Scheel, Schijen and Lakens 2021 (AMPPS 4(2)), which report shares of hypothesis-testing papers with full or partial support (about 84-86% in standard literature, 44% in Registered Reports; cited from memory, not re-checked here). These are method and framing claims, not the numbers, so 3 rather than 2.
evidence.fitness: Job: a researcher wants to know whether this agent-written portfolio buries failures, and to extend the measurement. They get a frozen snapshot, a reproducible random sample, the labels and the scripts, which is enough to start. They cannot reuse the labels as a measurement yet: the codebook exists only as one paragraph of README prose written while labelling, there is no second coder or kappa, long summaries were read truncated, and my spot-check moves about a quarter of the positive/negative labels. Nearest prior work: Fanelli 2010 and 2012 (share of papers reporting support for the tested hypothesis, coded from abstracts, with a codebook and a blind re-check of a subset), Scheel et al. 2021 (Registered Reports vs standard reports). The question asked of an agent-built portfolio is new as far as I know; the method is a smaller, weaker copy of theirs and the result is not compared with their numbers, which is the comparison a reader most wants (positive+mixed among tested here is 30/39 = 77% [62%, 87%], roughly comparable to Fanelli's 'full or partial support').
evidence.domain: Against content-analysis practice (a codebook fixed before coding, two coders, Cohen's kappa or Krippendorff's alpha reported, disagreements resolved; Fanelli's protocol), the study departs on every point and says so: a rubric fixed while labelling, one coder from the same model family that wrote many summaries, a keyword rule tuned on the evaluation set. The statistics are right for what they are (Wilson intervals on simple random sample proportions; the 23/39 interval is conditional on the 39, which the README states). The PhD bar in research/CLAUDE.md is not met: this is a well-documented pilot, not a measurement a methodologist would sign off as a finding.

defects.what: Labels depart from the stated rubric: three summaries with an explicit failure or 'but' clause (garment-stackopt, sensing-timesync, garment-twonodeheld) are labelled positive although the README says boundary cases went to the less flattering class; accel-fpga, accel-ttfit and tail-elicitation test no alternative; chip-mac-lanes confirms rather than refutes. A second reader moves the headline from 59% to about 71%. No codebook file and no second coder.

README says there is no comparable benchmark for the 59%, but Fanelli 2010/2012 and Scheel et al. 2021 publish shares of hypothesis tests reporting full or partial support from the same kind of abstract coding; the nearest prior work is cited for motivation only and the result is not compared with it.

The two headline computations are untested: run.py counting only 'negative' (dropping 'mixed') and removing a word from the DISCLOSE rule both leave all 7 tests green; nothing checks run.py output against results.txt.
'Boundary cases went to the less flattering class' is a method claim the labels do not back (see labels.tsv:7, :24, :67).

Titles are not passed through plain(), so 19 rows of data/summaries.tsv keep raw '’' entities, and the swe-orgs summary was snapshotted garbled ('checklistrsquo;s'); the JSON file handle is never closed.

verdict: A small, honest, reproducible pilot: every number in the README and homepage summary recomputes independently (Wilson intervals by quadratic roots, counts by awk, the confusion matrix by grep), run.py and the figure reproduce byte for byte, and the limitations are stated more candidly than most projects here. It does not meet the bar: verification is 2 (3 of 6 mutants survive, including the line that computes the 59% headline), and as research it is a single-coder, post-hoc-rubric content analysis that a meta-research methodologist would not accept as a measurement; a second reader disputes about a quarter of the positive/negative labels (moving the headline to about 71%) and the README's 'no comparable benchmark' overlooks Fanelli 2010/2012, the obvious comparison. The direction of the finding (the portfolio's comparative headlines are not mostly wins) survives the relabel.
